course_description:
Enrolment Note:This course has maximum quota of 25 students per semester, seminars with less than 10 students may not run. Enrolment for Seminars opens in O Week following the Honours Orientation information session. Enrolment will close once the quota has been reached.

This course provides students with the opportunity to gain in-depth knowledge of the primary research literature within the context of the wider theoretical framework in relation to relevant topics that vary from year to year.

Cyberpsychology and Cognitive Warfare

What happens when your mind is the target? This seminar explores how core principles of cognitive psychology can be used to understand decision-making, influence, and vulnerability in digital environments, and how these processes extend into offline or “real-world” contexts. The course takes a cognition-first approach, examining how people evaluate information, make decisions under uncertainty, and commit to actions when evidence is incomplete, ambiguous, or strategically shaped. Across the semester, we draw on established psychological models of decision-making and information processing and use these as lenses for understanding how such mechanisms are leveraged in phenomena such as persuasion, social engineering, online scams, and disinformation.

restrictions: BPsySc(Hons), BSc(Hons) in Psychology, BA(Hons) in Psychology students only.

course_aims: This course aims to develop skills in critical evaluation and to deepen understanding of contemporary research on a topic in psychology.

learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate a critical and in-depth understanding of key topics in an area of psychology.
Demonstrate an ability to communicate orally and in writing about a topic in an area of psychology.
Demonstrate an understanding of how different types of research methods can contribute to our understanding of an area of psychology.
Effectively engage with others to discuss and evaluate empirical research.

assessment_details.title: Seminar Presentation
assessment_details.due_date: 19/08/2026 - 28/10/2026 Presentation dates will be allocated in Week 1.
assessment_details.task_description: In small groups students will lead 40-60 minute group discussion based on an allocated weekly topic. Your presentation should not just summarise the topic, but should encourage the class to discuss larger issues/questions that arise from the topic. You are encouraged to draw on additional source material to supplement your presentation, if it would advance the discussion. The focus of this assessment is not just on your understanding of the topic but how effectively you are able to engage the group and facilitate collective learning and productive discussion during the session. Students may chose to incorporate class participation, group activities and question-and-answer style content. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Essay
assessment_details.task_description: The goal of the essay is to showcase your understanding of a topic that is germane to the materials covered in the course. Your essay (1500-2000 words) does not need to focus on a paper or topic that has specifically been covered in the course. The scope of your essay and the specifics of what you would like to cover will need to be negotiated with the course coordinator. Your essay must not have significant overlap with your presentation topic. Read full task description Hide full task description

The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking.

assessment_details.task_description: Active participation in the seminar sessions is essential for the course. Just as presenters will be expected to lead group discussion, audience members will be expected to engage with the speakers and discuss the material being presented in a thoughtful and constructive manner. Your participation in each session will be assessed on a pass/fail basis based on the quality (not quantity) of your contribution.
